case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). 3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

I think this is a severe case of inflammatory arthritis, likely a seronegative type given the negative labs and the poor response to methotrexate. My initial decision is to escalate to a biologic DMARD, like an anti-TNF agent, to try and control the aggressive synovitis and prevent further contractures. The recurrence post-surgery and the steroid-dependent, methotrexate-intolerant course really point toward needing stronger immunosuppression.

While aggressive synovitis is a concern, the poor response to methotrexate and steroids, along with the specific findings of nodular palmar tendon thickening and contractures without classic tenosynovitis, suggests we might be dealing with a non-inflammatory process. Before escalating to a biologic, we should consider a broader differential for rapidly progressive contractures, such as palmar fibromatosis or a systemic sclerosis mimic, given the normal inflammatory markers.

That's a good point. The normal inflammatory markers and the nodular tendon thickening do make a non-inflammatory cause more likely, especially since the synovitis on ultrasound was hypervascular but without effusions. Given that, maybe a deeper tissue biopsy from the palmar fascia would be more appropriate than jumping to a biologic.

Yes, a biopsy could be very informative. The rapid progression, contractures, and nodular thickening, despite negative serologies and normal inflammatory markers, are atypical for standard inflammatory arthritis and could point towards a fibrosing disorder like palmar fibromatosis or a systemic sclerosis variant.

I agree. A palmar fascia biopsy is the logical next step. The clinical picture with nodular tendon thickening, contractures, and lack of systemic inflammation really doesn't fit typical arthritis, and a tissue diagnosis is needed before committing to any further immunosuppression.

Agreed. Obtaining a tissue diagnosis is crucial to avoid unnecessary and potentially harmful immunosuppression. The biopsy can help differentiate between a localized fibrosing disorder like Dupuytren's disease and a systemic fibrosing condition.
Absolutely. Given the clinical picture and the risk of inappropriate immunosuppression, I'll arrange for a palmar fascia biopsy as the definitive next step.

I'll proceed with the biopsy as the definitive next step, as it aligns with the clinical evidence and prevents a misdirected treatment course.

I'll schedule the biopsy and hold off on any further immunosuppressants until we have the pathology results.

Perfect. That's a very safe and definitive plan. The biopsy will give us the definitive answer, and holding immunosuppressants is the right decision to avoid potential side effects for a non-inflammatory condition.
